title: India's 'cockroach' leaders jailed after holding protest
content: Two top leaders of India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) have been sent to jail for five days after being arrested for allegedly trespassing at a protest site in Delhi. Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka appeared before a magistrate on Wednesday after being detained at Jantar Mantar, a longstanding venue for demonstrations that police recently removed from the city's list of authorised protest sites. The two were among a group who climbed a locked gate and crossed barricades to enter the site on Tuesday. The GenZ-led movement has been protesting for days seeking electoral reforms and the resignation of India's top election official over allegations of vote fraud - charges the poll panel denies. Police accused Das, Ranka and their fellow activist Ajinkya Shinde of trespassing, breaching a peace bond, violating prohibitory orders and obstructing public officials - charges they deny. Delhi's Special Executive Magistrate Court remanded Das and Ranka to five days in judicial custody, while Shinde was released on a personal bond. The two leaders can seek bail from a higher court. Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi, who has been holding separate protests against the Election Commission, condemned the arrests, describing them as "an act of cowardice", and expressed support for peaceful demonstrations at Jantar Mantar. "Students. Youth. Journalists. The [opposition's] INDIA bloc. Different banners, one cause. All protests are one: citizens demanding their constitutional rights," he wrote on X. Other leaders of the opposition, like former chief ministers of West Bengal and Delhi- Mamata Banerjee and Arvind Kejriwal respectively - also took to X to extend support to CJP and condemn the arrest of its leaders. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, who was travelling to Delhi after the arrests, accused the government of cracking down on dissent and challenged Prime Minister Narendra Modi to "declare the Emergency officially", according to news agency PTI. His comments drew parallels with India's 1970s Emergency, a period when civil liberties were curtailed under then Prime Minister Indira Gandhi. The CJP, which is a pressure group and not an official political party, has been demanding the resignation of India's Chief Election Commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, over alleged irregularities in electoral rolls. Kumar and the Election Commission have denied wrongdoing. Wednesday's actions follow a weekend of protests during which Das, Ranka, Shinde, and Dipke were taken into preventive custody ahead of planned demonstrations at Jantar Mantar. They were later released by a magistrate. Police imposed extensive security restrictions across Delhi, closing several metro stations and deploying thousands of police and paramilitary personnel to prevent demonstrators from reaching the site. Thousands of people, including journalists, were detained and later released, while videos showed police forcibly dragging some protesters into buses. Following the weekend protests, Delhi police removed Jantar Mantar from its list of authorised protest sites, instead designating three other venues - Ramlila Maidan, Burari Ground and CBD Ground. The CJP criticised the decision, saying it would make demonstrations less visible and harder for protesters to make their voices heard. On Tuesday, the activists returned to Jantar Mantar despite the restrictions. Videos shared by Dipke and other CJP leaders showed Das and Ranka climbing over police barricades, carrying Indian flags and chanting slogans. "You cannot denotify the resistance," Dipke wrote on X. Ratna Singh, head of the CJP's legal team, alleged that the activists were denied access to lawyers for several hours before being taken to Parliament Street Police Station in a private vehicle at about 03:00 local time (21:30 GMT on Tuesday). She also rejected a police allegation that CJP leaders had called on others to join the protest at Jantar Mantar. "Absolutely false! No public call was ever made," she wrote on X. The CJP emerged from student-led demonstrations earlier this year over alleged exam irregularities and demands for education reforms. Weeks of protests led by the movement culminated in the resignation of federal Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The group began as an online satire movement after India's Chief Justice Surya Kant compared some unemployed young people to cockroaches during a court hearing in May. He later said his remarks had been misinterpreted, but the comments had already become a rallying cry for young people demanding change. Following the summer protests, the CJP developed into a wider pressure group, tapping into discontent over unemployment, examinations and government accountability. The CJP launched its latest nationwide protests in Mumbai on 2 October, following an Indian Express report alleging that Chief Election Commissioner Kumar had ignored objections from his two fellow commissioners over changes to voter registration. The newspaper reported that commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi had raised concerns at least 14 times over 10 months about decisions taken without their knowledge, including changes affecting voter databases and electoral rolls. The Election Commission has denied the allegations, saying its decisions were unanimous. The controversy has intensified scrutiny of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls, a voter verification exercise that opposition parties allege has benefited Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). The Election Commission and the government denies this. Although the CJP and opposition parties have not held joint protests, their demonstrations have coincided in recent days. Gandhi is among politicians, lawyers and journalists detained during protests across several cities. title: Australia's first-ever Michelin stars go to 11 restaurants in one state
content: Australia has been awarded its first Michelin stars, with 11 restaurants in the state of South Australia receiving the distinction. Magill Estate Restaurant in Adelaide was the only venue to receive two stars, while 10 others were awarded one star each. South Australia's government paid for incognito inspectors to visit the state, according to national broadcaster ABC, which is why no spots have been recognised in other parts of the country. Magill chef and owner Scott Huggins said he had "dreamt of working in Michelin star restaurants as a youngster". He said he had worked in Michelin star restaurants in Europe and Japan. "It's one thing working for one, one thing achieving two [Michelin stars]," he said. Wednesday's announcement comes more than a century after the Michelin Guide was first published in France and following years of unsuccessful attempts to bring it to Australia. Michelin has approached the national tourism board about bringing the guide to the country more than once, with no luck. South Australia decided to go it alone and pursued its own deal. The state government has not disclosed how much it paid, but Tourism Minister Emily Bourke defended the investment in an interview with ABC News. "It is enabling us to create a tourism destination and put us on the world map," she said. The move follows Michelin's expansion into New Zealand, which became the first destination in Oceania to feature in the guide in July, agreeing to pay NZ$6.3m (£2.7m; $3.5m) over three years for its inclusion. Created by brothers André and Édouard Michelin in 1900, the guide was originally designed to encourage motorists to travel - ultimately boosting their core business of selling tyres. It offered drivers maps and recommendations for places to eat and stay, before evolving into one of the best-known names in restaurant recognition. Michelin stars were introduced in 1926 and have since become a major distinction for chefs and restaurants around the world. One star recognises high-quality cooking, two stars indicate excellent cooking worth a detour, while three stars are reserved for exceptional cuisine worth a special journey. Among the one-star recipients is Arkhé in Norwood, which specialises in open-fire cooking, while Aptos in Adelaide serves a tasting menu focused on native Australian ingredients. title: India and China aren't friends - but Nepal wants to unite them against climate threats
content: Nepal's Prime Minister Balendra Shah used much of his speech at the recent UN General Assembly to warn of the growing threat of climate-related disasters in the Himalayas, recalling the devastating debris floods that struck his country in August. But it was his ambitious proposal to bring together regional rivals India and China, alongside Nepal, to tackle these shared threats that drew particular attention. Shah called for the creation of a Himalayan Climate Resilience Mechanism to strengthen cross-border disaster response and the sharing of scientific data and expertise in one of the world's most environmentally fragile and geopolitically sensitive regions. "Let the Himalayas become a laboratory of international co-operation rather than a frontier of fragmented information," he said. A senior official at Nepal's foreign ministry, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the proposal was still at an early stage. "The PM's proposal has given a political direction. Our ministry is working with other relevant agencies to put forward a preliminary framework which can be the basis for building common understanding," the official said. Neither India nor China has formally responded to the proposal. The BBC has contacted their foreign ministries for comment. But can Nepal really bring the two regional giants together to confront a shared climate threat in a region where they have long been locked in bitter territorial disputes? India and China share a disputed frontier stretching roughly 3,500km (2,175 miles), much of it across the Himalayas. Their competing territorial claims have led to a war, deadly clashes and repeated military stand-offs along the Line of Actual Control (LAC), the de facto boundary separating areas under their control. But the mountains that have long been a source of friction between the two countries are also facing an urgent climate threat. Temperatures in the Himalayan region are rising faster than the global average, accelerating glacier retreat and permafrost thaw and contributing to growing risks of landslides, rockfalls, avalanches and glacial lake outburst floods. Such disasters can sweep across national boundaries, threatening lives, infrastructure and livelihoods far downstream - making co-operation between the countries sharing the Himalayas increasingly important. A report by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development released in March found that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya (HKH) region are melting at an accelerating pace, with the rate of ice loss having doubled since 2000 compared with the 1974-1999 period. Further east, on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, glaciers have shrunk by 24% in area over the past six decades, Kang Shichang, director of the Chinese Academy of Sciences' Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment, told China's People's Daily Online. Experts say the retreat of glaciers can cause glacial lakes to expand, increasing the risk of sudden, potentially devastating floods that can cross borders into countries such as Nepal, India and Bhutan. Several major rivers flowing through these countries originate on the Tibetan Plateau. The plateau now has more than 14,000 glacial lakes, covering over 1,100 sq km, according to People's Daily. And the dangers extend beyond flooding. A 2024 study published by the American Geophysical Union projected a significant rise in landslide hazards across the Himalayas and Tibet in the coming decades due to increased rainstorms. While the largest absolute increases are expected in already vulnerable areas, including India's Garhwal and Kumaon regions and Nepal, the greatest relative increase is projected on the Tibetan Plateau. The growing risks make co-operation more urgent. But past efforts by India and China to work together on Himalayan environmental issues have made little progress. The two Asian powers have often found common ground at UN climate negotiations, pushing back against Western demands for emissions cuts and arguing that developing countries should not bear the same burden as industrialised nations. Yet they have no dedicated agreement to jointly address the impacts of climate change in the Himalayas. In 2009, India and China agreed to undertake joint research into the impact of global warming on glaciers in the Himalayas and Tibet. Following a visit to Beijing, India's then environment minister Jairam Ramesh announced that the Wadia Institute of Himalayan Geology and China's Cold and Arid Regions Environmental and Engineering Research Institute would collaborate on the project. But the initiative went nowhere, according to a scientist involved in the effort. "One meeting was held between us and the Chinese side and that was it, nothing came out of it," said Dr DP Dobhal, a retired glaciologist who headed the glaciology programme at the Wadia Institute. "What happened after that no one knows," he added. Since the early 2000s, India and China had agreements under which Beijing provided flood-season hydrological data on the Brahmaputra and Sutlej, two major rivers originating in Tibet. But in August 2025, India's junior foreign minister Kirti Vardhan Singh told parliament that both agreements had expired. China had stopped sharing data on the Brahmaputra in June 2023, while India had received no data on the Sutlej since 2022. China has not publicly explained the latest interruption. But when it withheld similar information in 2017, amid a tense military stand-off with India, Beijing blamed technical problems at its hydrological monitoring stations in Tibet, Singh said. Some analysts see a glimmer of hope in the recent thaw between India and China, marked by high-level political engagement and moves to revive cross-border trade through Himalayan routes. "These developments suggest there might be more room for the three countries to explore climate-related co-operation," says William Yang, senior analyst for North East Asia at the International Crisis Group. But he says Beijing is likely to remain cautious about any major agreement with India and Nepal, as border disputes remain unresolved. One major obstacle is that information vital for understanding climate risks can also have military value. "What climate scientists might see as essential research data might look like strategic intelligence to the national security establishment in an environment where two militaries face each other across a disputed frontier," says Walter Ladwig, an associate fellow in the Indo-Pacific Programme at the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI), a UK-based defence and security think tank. Such tensions have also hampered past efforts to tackle disasters that cross Himalayan borders. The Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD) has spent more than three decades promoting regional co-operation, including on flood early-warning systems. But progress has been slow. "There are certain highly sensitive issues in transboundary matters like comprehensive data of river flows that countries might not want to share, particularly upstream countries," says Arun Bhakta Shrestha, a former senior specialist at ICIMOD. He says countries should instead focus on sharing less sensitive information about disaster risks. Dr Uday Kala, head of the Centre for Climate Change and Disaster Management at India's IIT Mandi, suggests starting with practical steps - jointly identifying high-risk glacial lakes and cross-border hazards, agreeing on basic data-sharing protocols and monitoring standards, and exchanging critical warnings without delay. "Climate change is moving the baseline itself; catching up with the previous disaster is no longer enough. We need to anticipate the next one," he says. Whether India and China are willing to take even these steps remains uncertain. For Nepal, the challenge is to convince its two powerful neighbours to put aside their differences and work together to tackle a shared climate threat. title: Sally Rooney books withdrawn in UK over Palestine Action support
content: Normal People author Sally Rooney has said her novels will no longer be supplied to booksellers in the UK as a result of her support for Palestine Action. The Irish novelist said last year she intended to carry on using her royalties to support the group, which is a proscribed terrorist organisation in the UK. In a statement to BBC News, Rooney said further publication of her work could constitute a "serious criminal offence", so she had agreed with her publisher Faber not to continue supplying her books in the UK. "I have made every effort to be honest with the public about my beliefs and intentions, and I am wholly prepared to accept the consequences," she said. Ebook editions have already been removed from sale in the UK, although many book shops still have existing stock of physical copies. Waterstones confirmed to the BBC that Faber had advised there were no restrictions on booksellers keeping their current copies on the shelves. Rooney has sold more than six million books globally, including 2.3 million in the UK, according to NielsenIQ BookData. Normal People was released in 2018 and turned into a hit TV series two years later, effectively launching the acting careers of Paul Mescal and Daisy Edgar-Jones. Rooney's other novels are Intermezzo, Conversations With Friends and Beautiful World, Where Are You. Publisher Faber told BBC News: "Current legislation in the UK has led to circumstances where Faber cannot pass on UK earnings to Sally Rooney for her work. "To sell a writer's work and not be able to pass on earnings is an unconscionable situation for a publisher. "As such, and in full agreement with Sally, we have taken the decision that we can no longer supply her works in the UK in any format." Faber added: "We remain the proud publisher of her remarkable body of work, which we will continue to sell in other territories." The UK government proscribed Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation in 2025, saying it had a "long history" of criminal damage. The group's activities have included targeting arms companies linked to Israel's war in Gaza. In her statement on Wednesday, Rooney said: "In July 2025, the direct-action protest group Palestine Action was proscribed as a terrorist organisation in the UK. "The following month, I wrote an opinion piece expressing my intention to go on supporting Palestine Action, which is not a proscribed or otherwise prohibited group here in the Republic of Ireland." In her article last August in the Irish Times, Rooney said she would continue using proceeds from her work to support the group despite that being an offence in the UK, and cancelled a UK trip to pick up an award over fears she would be arrested. On Wednesday, Rooney continued: "As a result, the fulfilment of contracts to publish my work in the UK could now constitute a serious criminal offence. "After a process of consultation and deliberation, and with my full agreement, my publisher Faber has therefore determined that it can no longer supply my work within the UK." Palestine Action co-founder Huda Ammori said Rooney had taken "a brave and principled stand from the moment plans to ban Palestine Action were announced". Ammori said the author's work being withdrawn marked "a new low in the escalating assault on free speech caused by the proscription of Palestine Action". More than 3,700 people are believed to have been arrested in the UK over alleged support of Palestine Action. About 2,500 have been charged, although none have gone to trial as a legal challenge to the proscription continues and will be heard by the Supreme Court next month. title: Hidden video recording device found in cabin of Australian navy ship
content: A hidden video recording device has been found in an Australian navy ship's cabin, the Australian Defence Force (ADF) has confirmed. The device was located on Sunday in the cabin of Royal Australian Navy ship HMAS Leeuwin in Cairns, Queensland. The confirmation came after independent Australian senator Jacqui Lambie, a former veteran and defence advocate, told parliament she was contacted by personnel with allegations that "concealed cameras have recently been found in the female sailors' showers facilities". Australia's defence department has not said whether the device was found in a female-only space and said the incident was referred to the Joint Military Police United. Lambie told the Australian Senate on Wednesday: "I was also told this had occurred recently and prevented the vessel from sailing while investigations were ongoing. Even more disturbing are claims that footage from these cameras may have been uploaded online before the cameras were discovered. "How many of our female sailors have unknowingly been recorded in their most private moments? How much footage has been distributed online so far, retained or uploaded without knowledge or consent? These are the questions today I ask navy." Later on Wednesday, the defence department confirmed it became aware of a video recording device being found in a HMAS Leeuwin cabin but did not give specific details on where it was discovered. "Defence takes this incident extremely seriously and does not tolerate unacceptable behaviour in any form," the department said in its statement. "The ship remained alongside to enable the investigation and ensure immediate support was provided to members of the ship's crew. The welfare of individuals remains Defence's priority, and support is ongoing. "As the matter is currently under investigation and to protect the privacy of the affected individuals, Defence is unable to provide further comment at this time." title: Saudi Arabia overturns death sentence for man over Facebook comment, Sri Lanka says
content: Saudi Arabia's Supreme Court has set aside the death sentence handed to a Sri Lankan migrant worker over a comment he made on Facebook, Colombo's Deputy Foreign Minister Arun Hemachandra said. Anojan Sivarasa, 27, was sentenced to death in September after a Saudi appellate court convicted him of blasphemy against Islam and the Prophet Muhammad over his comment. The case sent shockwaves through Sri Lanka , spurring diplomatic efforts to seek clemency. Saudi Arabia's top court set aside the sentence on Wednesday, Hemachandra said in a post on Facebook, where he thanked the authorities and legal teams of both nations for their efforts. In late June, footage of a young Muslim man kicking a dog following Hindu pilgrims circulated widely on social media, triggering religious arguments online. During the exchange, a user posted derogatory remarks about a Hindu deity, leading Sivarasa to respond in Tamil insulting the Prophet Muhammad. Although Sivarasa promptly deleted the comment and posted an apology video, a screenshot of it was brought to the attention of his employer and Saudi officials, leading to his arrest in July. It is not clear if there will be further legal proceedings or whether Sivarasa will remain in detention, and for how long. He was initially sentenced to five years in prison as well as a fine of three million Saudi riyals ($0.8m; £0.6m) by the Al-Ahsa Criminal Court. Faizer Mustafa, a Sri Lankan lawmaker who is involved in legal negotiations with Saudi Arabia regarding Sivarasa's case, confirmed to BBC Sinhala that Saudi Arabia had overturned the death sentence, adding that they are reviewing the Supreme Court's latest ruling. Sivarasa's family had earlier said they have had no direct contact with him since 28 September. International rights groups had also joined calls for Saudi to spare his life. "Saudi authorities should end their use of abusive laws to hand out extraordinary sentences for speech-related offenses, especially against migrant workers who are already in a vulnerable position with limited protections," Joey Shea, senior Saudi Arabia researcher at Human Rights Watch, said on Tuesday. title: Russell Brand was a 'sexual predator', prosecution alleges as rape trial begins
content: Russell Brand was described as "ruthless" and a "sexual predator" by the prosecution at the start of his trial for rape and sexual assault on Wednesday. The 51-year-old actor and comedian faces three counts of rape, three charges of sexual assault and one of indecent assault. The allegations, made by six female complainants, span a 10-year period between 1999 and 2009. He denies the charges. Riel Karmy-Jones KC, for the prosecution, told Southwark Crown Court in London the women "did not know each other", "have never met each other" and "came forward independently of each other". The barrister said: "The circumstances of the offending were as wide and as varied as the defendant's career." She said that "regardless of who the women were and what they said or did, Brand was not deterred". "His desire, strong desire, for some form of sexual contact was indiscriminate and voracious," she told the court. The prosecutor told jurors that Brand would be "nice when he wanted to be, funny - undoubtedly - charming, likeable even, when he wanted something in return". But she said he would also be "demanding, entitled, a flirt with a huge sexual appetite - childlike in his expectation that his every desire should be met". The prosecutor said Brand would "appear indifferent, normal and untroubled by what had just occurred" after the encounters. She added that "sometimes he would leave promptly after the incident, sometimes making an excuse to get away, or sometimes simply continuing as though nothing wrong had happened". On Wednesday, the jury heard details of the alleged offences. The first complainant says she met Brand before he was famous in 1999, the jury was told. She had attended the Labour Party conference and went to a fringe event where she spoke to Brand. He later allegedly raped her. The prosecution said when Brand was questioned by police about this allegation of rape, "he said if it happened, he didn't remember the incident". He added that he did not remember the first complainant's name and that he "had never engaged in non-consensual activity". The second complainant worked for MTV at the time when she says Brand indecently assaulted her. She said Brand asked her where the toilets were and the woman offered to show him. When they reached the toilets, prosecutors say, Brand asked the woman to "come in" before grabbing her forearm. She resisted by struggling and pulling back. He had what she described as a desperate, wild-eyed look on his face, as he said: "Please please come in – oh go on." The third complainant says Brand orally raped her in a toilet after meeting her at a party in 2004. Within a minute of meeting, in the middle of a conversation, he lurched forward and grabbed her breasts and squeezed them with both hands, the jury was told. The prosecution said the woman remembered he had a "big, weird grin" on his face as he did so, then grabbed her arm and pulled her towards the toilets. The same woman said that as they were driving to another venue, Brand exposed himself, the court heard. "He said, 'Come on, come on, suck it' – to which she just said, 'No no'," the prosecution added. "He simply laughed but appeared to accept her refusal." The fourth complainant says Brand pushed her up against a wall at Capital Radio in 2004 or 2005 and kissed her "sloppily and aggressively", and "grabbed her body, at her breasts, sides and buttocks, aggressively". She was able to push him away and he "just sniggered, like it was a joke", the prosecutor said. The jury then heard how the fifth complainant says she met Brand when he was performing at the Hammersmith Apollo in London in 2009. The prosecution said their encounter began with consensual activity, but that he raped her anally on a later occasion. The jury heard how the woman "spent months and years blaming herself", becoming anxious and unwell. They were told Brand texted the woman after seeing her at an event the following summer, saying: "I wanna push you further." She is said to have replied: "I think you pushed me far enough – you treated me like an animal." He allegedly replied: "I'm sorry." The sixth complainant - who has accused Brand of sexual assault - says he demanded a massage when she was on a work assignment in 2009. He "fell to his knees and placed his head directly into her groin area", the prosecution said. After the accounts of the final two women were heard, the prosecutor said Brand told police in 2023 "he has never engaged in non-consensual sexual activity, and that any accounts had been reinvented or imagined after a defamatory documentary and subsequent press reporting". On Wednesday afternoon, Brand's former flatmate Mark Pinheiro was the first witness to give evidence. Pinheiro told jurors that Brand had told him he may have gone a "bit too far" with a woman when visiting the Labour Party conference in 1999. "He said that things got a little bit heated and a little bit out of hand, and he thinks that maybe he did go a little bit too far. "Those were his words - 'I think I may have gone a bit too far'." Pinheiro was pressed under cross-examination about whether he accurately remembered the comment, but he told the court he was sure Brand had said "things may have gone a little bit too far" or "I may have taken things a little too far". The trial continues and is expected to last for six weeks. Brand was accompanied by his wife Laura to the court on Wednesday. He rose to fame as a stand-up comedian and became a household name as host of TV shows such as Big Brother's Big Mouth, and with his own radio programmes on stations including BBC Radio 2 and 6 Music. He went on to establish a Hollywood career, starring in films including Forgetting Sarah Marshall and Get Him To The Greek. In recent years, he has turned to podcasting and now lives in Florida in the United States. The TV presenter says she suffered memory loss following her operation to remove a benign tumour. title: Brooklyn novelty shop reeling from 'surreal' row with Kelly Clarkson over mechanical bird
content: On a rainy Wednesday afternoon, a novelty toy and games store in the quiet Brooklyn neighbourhood of Cobble Hill was seeing much busier foot traffic than usual. Inside, the shop was packed with cameramen and customers, while passersby looked inside, asking: "Where's the bird?" Art of Play has found itself at the centre of a social media storm since the weekend when Grammy-winning musician Kelly Clarkson complained online that the boutique store would not let her buy a singing and dancing mechanical bird that was perched on the wall. The Since U Been Gone singer claimed she was "looked at as if I couldn't afford" the bird - which she said had a price tag of $15,000 (£11,000). "Y'all should go check out Art of Play in Brooklyn if you enjoy being treated like Julia Roberts' character in Pretty Woman," she said, referring to a scene from the 1990 romantic comedy film where Roberts' character is treated poorly by staff at a shop, who imply she cannot afford various items. In a follow-up post on social media, Clarkson said the store had told her the bird cost $15,000 and that they could find her something else "comparable". Art of Play has defended how it treated the star on social media, saying the wooden bird - which is called Molly - is permanently attached to the wall and is not for sale. It said that during Clarkson's five-minute visit on Saturday, an employee suggested to her that she could buy an identical bird for $15,000. They also said they had offered her a different singing bird for $2,000 from a clock-making shop in Germany, which she could have purchased that day. "Imagine our surprise when our small local business was suddenly attacked by eight million people who have never visited our store," Art of Play said. "It's been a surreal experience to be the focus of such widespread outrage after just one mention by a celebrity." Clarkson defended her decision to criticise the store on social media, saying: "I never blast people but you my friend were an exception." When the BBC visited the store on Wednesday, there were more reporters than customers. A shopkeeper said they would not comment on the story anymore and just wanted to get back to business as usual. Molly still hung on the wall at the shop, this time next to a price tag of $15m. The sign jokes that the sculpture is the "world's most famous singing bird automata!" The store's owner has said he and his staff have faced threats and harassment after Clarkson's complaint, telling the BBC's US partner CBS News that the singer had endangered them. This week, a man filmed himself yelling expletives outside the store, before accusing its employees of "racially profiling" Clarkson. The kerfuffle lingered in headlines on Wednesday as a news outlet released surveillance video from Art of Play purporting to show Clarkson's visit. The grainy footage, which has no audio, is said to show her wearing a yellow shirt, a baseball cap and a backpack while browsing items, including Molly the bird. She can be seen talking with an employee - apparently about the bird as she points at it - and later moving to leave the store. She comes back in to say something animatedly to the cashier. But while the argument over the bird has gone viral online, some of Art of Play's customers had not heard about it before being greeted by news cameras on the premises. One customer who was in town visiting his daughter said he was not familiar with the controversy. For others, Clarkson's claims that those at the store had treated her rudely came as a surprise. Kiran Ramineni, who lives next door, described Art of Play as a "very nice small mom and pop store" and said he had seen flocks of journalists there in recent days. Shopgoer Emily Trantanella, 27, said: "I feel like a pretty woman and I've always been treated very well here. "I really like it here." Naturalist Martin Gray says it is likely that the young guillemots lacked experience to deal with bad weather. The Royal Borough of Windsor & Maidenhead proposes "to explore new homes for the animals". A sharp increase in human activity is affecting the way the Himalayan monal lives and communicates, studies show. Researchers say the floating device acted as a deterrent for seabirds in the area. title: Russia arrests Japanese journalist on spying charges
content: Russian authorities have arrested a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage, accusing him of gathering information related to Moscow's defence capabilities for Tokyo. The journalist, identified as Yuki Imai from the Hokkaido Shimbun newspaper, was detained in the far-eastern Sakhalin region, a day before he was due to leave Russia. He was flown to Moscow where a court ordered he be placed in pre-trial detention, Russian reports say. Japan says it is still seeking details about the arrest, and has not been able to contact Imai. The arrest comes as tensions worsen between the two nations after Russian leader Vladimir Putin visited the disputed Kuril Islands , claimed by both countries, in August. Russian authorities allege that Imai "acted on the instructions of [Japan's] national intelligence service" to gather information about people involved in a special military operation on the Kuril Islands, state news agency TASS reported. The Kuril islands sit between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. The archipelago is administered by Russia, but four of the southernmost islands are claimed by Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories. Russia's FSB security agency published footage showing three masked men in black uniforms storming a hotel room and handcuffing a man. The video then shows him being accompanied onto a plane before appearing in a cage in a Moscow court. It did not say when he was detained or when the court hearing took place. Imai will be remanded until 12 December, before his trial begins, according to Interfax, another Russian news agency. Those convicted of espionage in Russia can be sentenced to up to 20 years in prison. "Tokyo's attempts to use its correspondents in Russia, who hold foreign journalist status, to gather information aimed at undermining our country's security are regrettable," Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said in a statement on Tuesday. "We cannot help but point out that today's incident is not an isolated one," she noted, but did not name other journalists or media outlets that are allegedly involved in similar activity. Japan has not commented at length on the arrest. Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a press briefing that Japan did not know about the arrest until the announcement and had had no contact yet with the journalist. Imai's published work has covered Russia's relations with North Korea and life in Sakhalin. Hokkaido Shimbun ran a report on the arrest without naming the reporter. "We are still confirming the details. Ensuring the reporter's safety is our top priority," it said in response to the BBC's queries. Russia and Japan have been locked in a dispute over the Kurils for decades, and it is the main reason Moscow and Tokyo did not sign a peace treaty after World War Two. Japan's Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi sharply criticised Putin's visit – his first-ever to the islands – saying it "wounded the feelings of the Japanese people" and is "incompatible with Japan's consistent position on the Northern Territories". Moscow dismissed her remarks as "politically inappropriate" and "legally unfounded". Over the years, attempts to resolve the territorial dispute have made little progress. Bilateral ties have also remained frosty, with Japan imposing sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Last week, Moscow again angered Tokyo by requesting the extradition of the president of the International Criminal Court (ICC), who is Japanese. The president Tomoko Akane, along with other ICC officials, has been placed on Russia's wanted list since 2023 after the court issued an arrest warrant for Putin over war crimes in Ukraine. In 2023, Russia detained The Wall Street Journal's Evan Gershkovich on espionage charges and later sentenced him to 16 years in prison. Gershkovich, a US citizen, was released in a 2024 prisoner swap, the largest exchange since the Cold War ended in 1991. In 2019, Moscow detained an unnamed Japanese journalist from Kyodo News on suspicion of attempting to obtain military secrets. The journalist, who was picked up in Vladivostok, was ordered to leave the country within 72 hours. Additional reporting by Chie Kobayashi Four years after the attacks, Serhii Kuznetsov appears in court accused of a plot to destroy Russia's gas pipelines to Germany. Elon Musk's system allows Kyiv to protect Ukrainian skies and effectively guide drones to Russian targets. BBC Ukraine Correspondent Dan Johnson is in Kyiv, where at least three people were killed in overnight strikes. It comes after Andy Burnham said Moscow had tried to interfere in the 2016 referendum. title: I'm 12 and I want to try protein powder - should I?
content: Twelve-year-old Ben is desperate to try protein powder but there's one hurdle: me, his mum. "I've asked about 20 times and you just keep saying no!", he says, claiming it would make him "fitter and bigger" and that his male friends use it. In recent years, there's been an explosion of products marketed as "high protein", including milk, yoghurt, breads, cereals, bars and powders. Social media is flooded with adverts for various supplements, including protein powder. As a health journalist, I'm sceptical and think at Ben's age he must be getting enough protein through his diet. So, do experts think it's safe for pre-teens and teenagers or is a big, juicy steak just as good? My sport-obsessed son, who already eats a healthy balanced diet, asks me about protein powder on a regular basis. His friend Louis, 12, has been using protein powder once or twice a week for nearly a year, after a workout and on top of whole foods. His parents are aware of this. "I think it's helped, it gives me more energy and it's helped me grow, probably," he says. But Ben's other friend Otis, who is 13, is not keen on the idea and feels there is pressure on young people to take protein supplements. "They might just start using them without thinking about the consequences or what effects it may have on them." Proteins break down into amino acids that help the body grow and repair. But your body can't make all the amino acids it needs on its own, so you need to get more - known as essential amino acids - through your diet. For an adult with a healthy weight, the recommended daily amount of protein you should be eating is 0.75 grams per kg of body weight, according to the NHS. A good rule of thumb is that the amount of protein you have for each meal should fit into the palm of your hand. If you exercise a lot, and when you get older, you need more protein so you could have up to 2 grams per kg of body weight. But do teens really need it if they're eating well? For teenage boys and girls "you can get all the protein that you need from food alone", says registered dietitian Nichola Ludlam-Raine. It is important that teenage girls, especially, get enough iron and calcium, so Ludlam-Raine says not to become overly focused on protein at the expense of other nutrients. Protein shakes, powders or bars can be useful for some, including high-level athletes and those who have certain allergies, but they should not replace a healthy diet. There can also be some unwanted side effects from using protein powders such as bloating, gas, cramps, and diarrhoea. Those with pre-existing health conditions should not use it unless they have been told they can by their doctor. Ludlam-Raine points out that the protein powder market is not as tightly regulated as medicines. "Of course, you can get reputable companies who do third-party testing and make sure that what you see on the label is what is in the inside, but that's not always the case," she says. "And ultimately you can't just have a shake and your biceps grow." Some protein powders contain high amounts of added sugar, artificial ingredients, and hidden stimulants. Dr Ramnik Mathur is a consultant paediatrician from Chelsea and Westminster NHS Trust. He explains that we need micronutrients like zinc, calcium and magnesium, which are found in whole foods. So, if meals are replaced with protein shakes, those nutrients are lost. Experts suggest spreading out protein across the day and aiming for 20-25g per meal. If you're keen to up your intake, try some of these recipes. During puberty when children have growth spurts, they do need more protein because their body is growing rapidly, building new muscle and bone mass. But Mathur says there are risks to eating too much protein. "If you look at social media, they'll say you need to eat a lot of protein, but your body can handle only so much." He explains that if you eat too much, it has to be excreted by the kidneys and liver which can become overloaded. Mathur explains: "We had a child here at the hospital where I work - he was taking so much protein that his kidneys just stopped working and he actually passed away." The key takeaway from Mathur: "If a 12-year-old child is eating a healthy balanced diet then they shouldn't need any more protein." Ludlam-Raine's advice is to get teens to improve their diet first before taking any protein powder, especially regularly. If they still want to use it, speak to a registered dietitian or nutritionist first. Now off I go to tell my son the answer is still no - and the experts say the same. Copyright 2026 BBC. title: Watch: Hong Kong crowds queue to see Van Gogh painting unveiled for first time in 60 years
content: One of Vincent van Gogh's paintings not seen publicly for more than 60 years has drawn crowds in Hong Kong, where it has been displayed ahead of auction this weekend in New York. Van Gogh painted Châtaigniers en fleurs (Chestnut Trees in Blossom) in the French village of Auvers-sur-Oise, about two months before he died in 1890. Sotheby's estimates the painting will fetch $180m (£136m), which would mark the highest auction price for a Van Gogh artwork. The critically endangered apes were rescued from intense wildfires that destroyed their habitat in August and September. title: Why Zelensky's meeting with Burnham matters
content: Prime Minister Andy Burnham welcomed President Volodymyr Zelensky to Downing Street on Wednesday, as the Ukrainian leader looks to shore up his European allies five years into Russia's war on Ukraine. Burnham told Zelensky that Britain "would forever stand by you" and that he was accelerating the delivery of air defences to Ukraine. Burnham previously told MPs that he would try to "repair bridges" between Ukraine and the United States and that Ukraine won't leave "empty-handed". The two leaders met at No 10 Downing Street where Zelensky was welcomed with a military ceremonial guard - thought to be a first for a foreign leader. BBC World News correspondent Joe Inwood explains what we know about the meeting. Read more about the meeting in London. The new prime minister told Laura Kuenssberg that people "voted for a manifesto" that he would honour, when pressed on whether there will be an early general election. See inside Andy Burnham's first week in charge, with an exclusive behind the scenes look with Laura Kuenssberg. After becoming PM on Monday, Burnham appointed John Healey as chancellor, Ed Miliband as foreign secretary and Wes Streeting as defence secretary The BBC's Annita McVeigh talks us through some key appointments as Andy Burnham takes office. The BBC's Sarah Smith looks at how the new UK prime minister will manage his most crucial, and perhaps the trickiest, international relationship. title: Container ship hit by projectile sinks in Strait of Hormuz, Singapore says
content: A Singapore-flagged container ship has sunk after being struck by an unknown projectile while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Singaporean authorities. All 21 crew members of GFS Pride were evacuated and no injuries were reported after the attack on Tuesday, which caused damage and a fire, the Maritime and Port Authority of Singapore said. Another Singapore-flagged container vessel, GFS Giselle, sustained hull damage after being hit by a projectile on Wednesday but was able to reach a safe anchorage with all 22 crew, it added. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a ship hit naval mines and sank while passing through what they called an "unauthorised" route in the Strait of Hormuz. The Guards released photos that appeared to show a plume of black smoke rising from a container vessel that was still afloat but down by the stern. In other photos, dozens of containers and their contents could be seen floating in the water. The Hydrographer of Pakistan warned mariners that GFS Pride had sunk 4 nautical miles (7.4km) north-west of Ras al-Sheikh Masud in Oman's Musandam Peninsula. Meanwhile, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said that two unnamed container ships had reported being struck by unknown projectiles while transiting the Strait of Hormuz between 16:40 and 17:00 GMT on Tuesday. Both vessels sustained minor damage and were able to continue their passages, it added. Merchant vessels have come under repeated attack in the Strait of Hormuz - which connects the Gulf to the Gulf of Oman and Arabian Sea - and elsewhere in the Middle East since the US and Israel's war with Iran began in February. At least 24 seafarers have been killed in 106 confirmed incidents, according to the UN's International Maritime Organization. The Malta-flagged container ship Safeen Prestige, which was attacked near Oman on 4 March, is the only other vessel reported to have sunk in that time. However, maritime risk management group Vanguard said on Wednesday that the Antigua and Barbuda-flagged bulk carrier Cape Dao was reported to be sinking after an unsuccessful rescue attempt, according to Reuters news agency. One seafarer was killed when the Cape Dao's bridge and accommodation area were hit by an unknown projectile as it transited through the Strait of Hormuz, north-east of Khasab, Oman, on 23 September. The Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas shipments usually pass, was effectively closed after the start of the Iran war due to Iranian missile and drone attacks on commercial vessels and a US naval blockade of Iranian ports. The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. Iran insisted it would not give up some measure of control over the waterway and began targeting vessels using a southern route through Omani waters that avoids its preferred route through Iranian waters. To keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states, the US military has been providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the Strait of Hormuz. Last month, crude exports through the waterway rose to around 80% of pre-war levels of 16 million barrels per day (bpd) on average, according to analysts from shipping data company Kpler, despite an increase in attacks on shipping. The Windsor Castle state visit will be the first for a Sultan of Oman in the UK since 1982. BBC Security Correspondent Frank Gardner analyses what intelligence agency's boss said in his annual speech and what it means for Britain. The prime minister says Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard "almost certainly" directed the RAF Fairford incident. A £60m investment has seen four of Europe's biggest quay cranes delivered to Southampton docks. title: 'Keeping spirits up for both of them': Pope's brother also receiving cancer treatment, wife says
content: The wife of Pope Leo XIV's brother says her husband is also receiving treatment for cancer after the Vatican announced the Pope has the disease. Deborah Prevost, the wife of the Pope's eldest brother, Louis Prevost, told CBS News, the BBC's US partner, on Tuesday that her husband has a form of blood cancer. It is unclear how advanced it is. Her comments came on the same day that Pope Leo, 71 - the first US-born head of the Catholic Church - underwent what the Vatican described as "successful" surgery for lung cancer. He is expected to remain in hospital for a week. Deborah Prevost said the family was "going through a lot" and that they are "keeping spirits up for both of them". She said her husband was being treated for multiple myeloma as part of a clinical trial at a hospital in Florida where they live. He was first diagnosed with cancer in 2017 and had undergone treatment in 2019, but "fell out of remission" three months ago. Multiple myeloma affects the blood, bone marrow, and can impact kidneys, according to a factsheet by the UK's National Health Service (NHS). It is not currently considered curable but the Multiple Myeloma Research Foundation says on its website that survival rates have significantly improved in the past decade. Louis Prevost confirmed his cancer diagnosis in a separate interview with US news outlet Newsmax, saying he was undergoing CAR-T cell therapy. This involves reprogramming a patient's immune cells to recognise and destroy blood cancers, the NHS states. Louis Prevost told Newsmax's Finnerty programme that it had been a shock to learn his brother also had cancer. "I got a message from his right hand that he was out of surgery, awake, feeling good, and was in no pain," he said of the Pope's condition. "So, we were all in high hopes and high spirits hoping for the best." Deborah Prevost said the brothers spoke last week as her husband prepared to go to hospital. "He called to let us know what would be happening," she said. The Pope announced on Sunday he would be operated on "in the coming days" after a nodule was found on his lung during a medical check-up. "We keep praying, keeping spirits up for both of them," said Deborah Prevost. The Pope, whose birth name is Robert Francis Prevost, underwent a 90-minute surgery on Tuesday at Rome's Gemelli Hospital and was subsequently diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma - a type of cancer usually found in the outer part of the organ. During the surgery, a lower lobe of his right lung was removed, the church said in a medical bulletin. "The operation was successful and there were no complications," the Vatican said. "After the operation, the Pope awoke normally and returned after a brief period of observation to his room." The pontiff had a "peaceful night" in the hospital, the Vatican said on Wednesday morning. Adenocarcinomas develop in cells that produce mucus and are one of the most common types of lung cancer. The long-term prognosis depends on a number of things, including the stage of the cancer when identified and the person's overall health. The earlier it is spotted, the better, and treatments have improved over the last few decades. Some adenocarcinomas are picked up early - before symptoms develop - during routine tests. At later stages, lung cancer can cause a persistent cough, breathlessness, fatigue and weight loss. Caroline Bailey was diagnosed after suffering with "a stabbing pain in the middle of my abdomen". The Scottish athlete, who has inoperable brain tumours, previously made a tearful plea for more investment in brain cancer research on BBC Breakfast. A coroner warns there's a risk of future deaths due to "substantial delays" in ophthalmology follow-ups. The 71-year-old Pope was diagnosed with lung cancer after the 90-minute procedure on Tuesday.
