title: Greenland contradicts Trump’s claim that ‘massive’ oil and gas drilling is about to begin there
content: Greenland’s government pushed back against President Donald Trump’s claim on Wednesday that “massive oil, gas and mineral exploration is getting ready to begin” in the Arctic territory. While Greenland’s deputy mining minister Jørgen Hammeken-Holm acknowledged that “there are activities by US companies,” he told CNN that “we are very far away from ‘massive’ exploration.” “There are many smaller explorations underway but these could take years to become operational,” he added, echoing researchers who have pointed out the difficulties and enormous expense involved in extracting resources from Greenland. The Foreign Ministry of Denmark, of which Greenland is an autonomous part, said that if the US wants to explore Greenland’s resources, it would have to do so within the Arctic Island’s legislation. Denmark also said the US-Denmark-Greenland agreement signed last month did not change this. “The agreement does not grant investors from the US any preferential treatment compared with investors from other NATO countries, EU countries and NATO partners when it comes to access to natural resources in Greenland,” it added. Many of the island’s deposits are located in remote areas above the Arctic Circle, where there is a mile-thick polar ice sheet and little infrastructure. Approximately 80% of the island is covered in ice. Since returning to the White House, Trump has repeatedly threatened to take control of Greenland and its natural resources, angering European and NATO partners. “There are experts that are saying that the amount of easily available oil is far greater than that of almost any land, anywhere in the world,” Trump wrote on Truth Social in the early hours of Wednesday. Later in the day, he claimed that the media exaggerated his ambitions for Greenland and that he was never considering taking the Arctic island by force. “You know, we took a lot of heat from the fake news back there,” Trump said at a rally in Arizona. “They said, ‘What a terrible way to talk about Greenland! This is terrible.’ Remember, they thought I was going to send my military out to attack Greenland. I wasn’t, but I complained about it very strongly to NATO, and really strongly,” he added. For years, Trump had suggested annexing the self-governing territory . Shortly before taking office for his second term in 2025, he didn’t rule out seizing Greenland by force , claiming it was vital for US security. Earlier this year, however, he ruled out military action in remarks to the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland . Last month the US, Denmark, and Greenland reached an agreement intended to help resolve tensions following Trump’s threats to annex the strategically located island. The agreement, which Trump claimed at the time gave the US “permanent control” over Greenland’s security, begins with an acknowledgment of Denmark’s sovereignty and Greenlanders’ right to self-determination. The agreement, which makes small changes to a 1951 treaty that gives the US permission to station troops in Greenland as part of NATO’s defense, makes no explicit mention of oil or gas, but acknowledges “minerals cooperation” and “cooperation on economic development and business promotion,” with no further specifics, according a text of the agreement published on the White House’s website. It also paves the way for additional US bases, and an assurance of US military access if Greenland becomes independent from Denmark. In his post on Wednesday, Trump said, “Any future attack on the United States will have to come across Greenland, where our Defense will routinely knock down drones, missiles, or any other form of weapon not yet even conceived.” CNN has reached out to the White House, to the Danish Prime Minister’s Office, and to Greenland’s Mineral Resources Authority for comment.

title: Exclusive: Judge limited Justice Department access to Rep. Ilhan Omar’s records in sprawling immigration fraud probe
content: The Trump administration pushed for an unusually aggressive search of Rep. Ilhan Omar ’s house in recent days in an immigration fraud probe that targets the congresswoman, possible false statements made on government documents, and a potential conspiracy, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation. Prosecutors, however, first had to contend with a federal magistrate judge, in a prolonged back-and-forth that hasn’t previously been reported. Judge Matthew Sharbaugh of the DC District Court ultimately limited how the Justice Department could access Omar’s documents in Monday’s search, before he would approve the warrant, because of her role as a member of Congress and the Constitutional protections that affords, multiple people familiar with the investigation told CNN. The investigators’ inquiries that prompted the search include whether Omar or her now-deceased father lied about her age when she obtained citizenship in 2000, claiming she was a minor when she was of adult age. Omar emigrated to the US as a Somalian refugee around the age of 12 and became a citizen in 2000, according to people familiar with Omar’s situation. One source told CNN the government could try to expand the investigation into a wider conspiracy case and try to investigate if this was deception and the purposeful falsification of information over years by a larger group of individuals. Omar has been under criminal investigations for years — including before Trump took office last year. But the Trump administration has pushed further with the belief that she has repeated false statements when filling out government documents, such as a passport, in recent years. That is what led to the search on Monday, the sources say. The search of her home in DC was highly unusual for its timing less than a month before Election Day voting ends, including while Omar is running for reelection as a Democrat in Minnesota. The effort is also the federal push this month has also been unusual for its attempt to access a member of Congress’ records — the type of criminal investigative work that Republicans this year have made into a political firestorm for past administrations. As part of the renewed probe, at least a dozen subpoenas were issued beginning last Friday to witnesses, most of them relatives, according to people familiar with the investigation. Government records and archives in Somalia are notoriously unreliable and hard to access due to years of conflict and disconnected government entities. In recent weeks, the Justice Department argued for broad access to records that Omar kept at her home in Washington, the sources said. The Justice Department has argued that with Omar there was little need for sequestering the records taken from her home on Monday. But the judge who ultimately approved the search told the Justice Department that wasn’t possible under the law, the sources said. Sharbaugh of the DC District Court told prosecutors from DC they would need to set up a process for screening the records to protect Omar’s legislative work from investigators. In DC, the courts have upheld expansive protections around records of legislative work for members of Congress under the Constitution’s Speech or Debate Clause. The multi-day back-and-forth between the judge and the Justice Department in recent days hasn’t been previously reported. It may now have vast implications for both federal investigators that are looking to potentially charge Omar with a crime and for her campaign. The Justice Department’s approach to the search also was especially notable because Omar, a US citizen originally from Somalia, is a high-profile member of the group of female progressives known as “The Squad,” a top and frequent political target of President Donald Trump and is running for re-election to Congress in Minnesota, where voting in the mid-term elections has already begun. Omar has publicly called the search of her home a political attack prompted by the hatred that Trump and Republicans have for her. “This is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” Omar said in a post on social media on Monday. “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation.” She has denied any wrongdoing and hasn’t been charged with a crime. An attorney for Omar didn’t respond to multiple requests for this story. Investigators are looking into an unsubstantiated claim around whether her now ex-husband, Ahmed Nur Said Elmi, was her brother, in order to get him citizenship — a claim that has been repeated by Trump and which Omar has called “bigoted lies.” Even if substantiated, the statute of limitations would have long run out over any crime, and it’s unclear what role that would play in the inquiry, informed sources told CNN. No charges were brought by the Biden-era investigators and the case around Omar didn’t progress nearly as far as the current Trump-era investigators have taken it, several people familiar with the investigation said. The case was reopened last year and is now being led by prosecutors in the deputy attorney general’s office and in the US attorney’s office in Minneapolis, the sources said. The US Attorney’s Office in Washington, DC, has also been involved. Any new case, if charged, would likely be complicated by Trump’s rhetoric against Omar, over many years and some of it being racist. Vice President JD Vance has also talked about discussing the case with White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, and White House border czar Tom Homan has repeatedly talked on Fox News about an ongoing investigation into Omar. “If someone committed immigration violation, someone committed marriage fraud or anything like that, regardless if they’re a congressman or not, no one’s above the law, so I’ll leave it at that,” Homan said in a September interview after mentioning an “ongoing criminal investigation” around Omar. A separate investigation of possible financial misconduct, including around campaign finance, also continues in the DC US attorney’s office. DC US Attorney Jeanine Pirro was asked on Tuesday on Fox News about Omar’s financial disclosures that House ethics investigators previously scrutinized. “That is the subject of an investigation as well,” Pirro said. “We’re looking at the facts. Based upon the facts we will follow them wherever they take us.” Since the DC federal court’s oversight of the search of Omar’s home, any criminal investigation that would rely on her own records may be slowed down substantially, and has already raised concerns about Justice Department integrity and politicization. Judges in the DC District Court have grown increasingly skeptical of the Trump administration’s approach to Constitutional protections in criminal cases, especially when those cases appear politically charged. At the same time, Republicans have been furious with the Justice Department under President Joe Biden for seeking Congress members’ communications in past criminal investigations. Republicans on Capitol Hill and Trump have been particularly critical of former special counsel Jack Smith obtaining secrecy orders when Smith’s office subpoenaed phone companies for call logs of members around the January 6, 2021, US Capitol attack conspiracy investigation. Generally, the Justice Department avoids overt investigative activity that could affect an election within 60 days of Election Day. In this case, however, top Justice officials signed off on Monday’s HSI search.

title: Trump admin silent as Russia hits American businesses with ‘drones and missiles’ in Ukraine
content: As President Donald Trump and his administration have ratcheted up pressure on Ukraine to stop striking Russian refineries, citing harm to American consumers, they have remained silent on recent Russian strikes on US businesses in Ukraine. Russia has escalated its attacks on facilities tied to American corporations – and civilian infrastructure in Ukraine writ large – over the past several months. According to Andy Hunder, the President of the American Chamber of Commerce in Ukraine, Russian missiles and drones have damaged facilities belonging to some of America’s most notable brands, including Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, McDonalds and Oreo. Although Russia has tried to deter successful American business in the past, it’s “nothing we’ve seen like over the last months,” Hunder told CNN. “This is a direct hit with drones and missiles, and they keep hitting them. It’s sending a message that they’re targeting American business. We’re not seeing any response from the White House,” he said. “We need this to stop because these are American interests, American money, American investors that are being hit and are being targeted,” he said. When a Russia drone struck a Coca-Cola factory outside Kyiv in early September, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attack was a “clear signal” to the US. “Today, the Russians struck a Coca-Cola plant with a drone. Coca-Cola has become such an enemy to them that they’re burning it down with their Shaheds,” Zelensky said in his nightly video address on September 3, referring to “Iranian-designed ​drones.” “This is a clear signal from Russia to America. The Russians cannot possibly be unaware that this is an American enterprise,” Zelensky added. Later that month, the Russians used “an attack drone” to destroy a warehouse used by McDonald’s, Zelensky said in a post on X . McDonald’s Ukraine confirmed in a statement that “a warehouse operated by one of our logistics partners in the Kyiv region was damaged in a drone attack on 25 September.” “An attack drone – against ordinary food products,” he wrote. “The Russians are constantly expanding their escalation operation: American and other businesses, data centers, internet providers – for Russia, ordinary life in and of itself is simply a target.” McDonald’s Ukraine said that as a result of the damage, its restaurants are offering a reduced menu. PepsiCo acknowledged in a statement in late August that a production facility in the Mykolaiv region was damaged, but there were no casualties. There is not a consensus among the US businesses on the ground about how much they want to talk publicly about being hit “or disclose the fact that they’ve been targeted multiple times,” a former senior State Department official told CNN. “Some businesses do want us to raise this,” Hunder echoed, but others “are treading very carefully.” However, several Democratic US lawmakers have publicly called on the White House to do more to protect American businesses in Ukraine and to call out Moscow’s actions. Ukraine has highlighted the attacks as another reason to step up defense support, so that they can sufficiently shield American companies on the ground. The Chamber of Commerce meets with visiting US lawmakers from both parties when they visit Kyiv, and Hunder told CNN they have asked them to raise the matter with the White House. President Donald Trump spoke out publicly when asked in August 2025 about a Russian strike on a US electronics factory, saying he told Russian President Vladimir Putin that he was “not happy about it.” A White House official said Trump “wants the war to stop entirely so the senseless killing ends.” “The president and his team remain committed to continuing to play a constructive role in ending the war between Russia and Ukraine, and he remains optimistic that we’ll ultimately get a peace deal done,” the official said, arguing that the US is “the only country in the world” that can “play a constructive role in speaking to both sides in working towards bringing the war to an end.” Still, the relative lack of condemnation on the strikes from the Trump administration stands in contrast to the admonishments to the Ukrainian government about striking Russian energy infrastructure. In February, CNN reported the administration had warned Kyiv that its strikes on a Russian Black Sea oil facility late last year had impacted US investments in Kazakhstan. In recent weeks, Trump has blamed Ukraine’s strikes on Russian diesel facilities for rising fuel prices, which have been driven up by the US-Iran war. Last Friday, he announced a deal to waive sanctions and purchase diesel from Russia, in defiance of US law. The US has also threatened to restrict intel sharing and munitions for Ukraine if Kyiv does not stop those strikes, sources told CNN. Hunder told CNN he has struggled to understand the administration’s relative silence on the matter, particularly given how much they’ve portrayed themselves as pro-US business. “Any company, any business, wants to have some sort of protection. You would expect your government to stand up in your corner and fight the fight with you, especially if it’s a foreign military that is attacking the American companies,” he said. The former senior State Department official noted that “there’s an awful lot of people in ‘official Washington’ who think the only people who can talk about Ukraine are Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, and if it’s not one of the two of them, then we need to stay out of it.” As such, it is a challenge to even draw attention to the attacks on US businesses. “The idea that you would get a rationale back” on why the US was silent about the attacks “is not something that people can expect,” they told CNN. Hunder said the American Chamber of Commerce sent a message seeking a meeting with Witkoff and Kushner last month to update them on the state of US business in Ukraine, including the latest hits on American business. “We didn’t get any response on that,” he said.

title: Democrats have reason to be optimistic, but headaches could be waiting if they win the midterms
content: If Democrats win the Senate next month, the chamber’s new swing voters will likely be an interesting cast. They’ll be Democrats from states that voted for President Donald Trump by double digits, and who have distanced themselves from their party on transgender rights, oil drilling, immigration and even the left’s desire to scrutinize the Trump administration. And some of them are anxious to tout their willingness to work with the president. Democratic leaders did a good job recruiting and helping nominate candidates with moderate brands whom voters seem to like . That’s helped them compete on a difficult map where the party needs to win at least two states Trump won by double digits to nab the majority. But if Democrats nab that majority, the party will face a challenge in trying to balance the interests of some of these new moderate lawmakers with the demands of the base. One of the most common issues where these moderate candidates have tacked to the right has been transgender athletes. Opposition to allowing transgender students to play on girls’ sports teams — or some version of that position — has been embraced by state Rep. Josh Turek in Iowa, state Rep. James Talarico in Texas, pastor Adam Hamilton in Kansas and physician Annie Andrews in South Carolina. Both Talarico and Andrews had previously embraced a broader version of transgender rights and spoke out on behalf of that community. But after Trump attacked Andrews using an anti-transgender slur , the South Carolina Democrat filmed a direct-to-camera ad in which she said, “I don’t support biological men playing women’s sports and I don’t support — and haven’t ever performed — gender surgery for minors.” She added in a debate on Sunday: “ I don’t support gender surgery on minors .” Hamilton added the same day on ABC’s “This Week”: “I believe that there are two biological genders .” Another significant break from the national party has been on immigration. “Democrats have failed on the border,” Andrews said at the debate. Talarico has said that “Joe Biden and his administration failed us on our southern border .” Alaska Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola has run an ad touting her votes breaking with her party on the border, including being one of just six House Democrats to symbolically condemn then-Vice President Kamala Harris and the Biden administration’s border policies in 2024. Turek has also repeatedly returned to that theme, including launching a new ad this week featuring a sheriff saying Turek “broke with his party and voted with Republicans to support law enforcement … and crack down on illegal immigration.” He indeed voted with just a few Democrats to make being in the country illegally a state crime in Iowa . Other areas of separation are a bit more state specific. One of Peltola’s big issues is increased oil and gas production. The Alaska Democrat also touts her “A” rating from the National Rifle Association. Hamilton has also decried the “ war on domestic energy projects ” The Kansas Democrat even said he’d consider a temporary diesel export ban, which Trump floated and then later ruled out, to hopefully lower prices (despite experts being skeptical of the idea). And Hamilton also recently suggested he’s not overly keen on some Democrats’ desire to investigate Trump administration officials — saying he instead prefers to institute “guardrails.” “I’m not going to Washington to hold trials,” he told MS NOW . “I’m going to Washington to fight for the people of Kansas and make life better for them.” That could seemingly be a problem if that kind of accountability becomes a major focus for a potential Democratic majority. (That would likely be where much of Democrats’ energy is devoted since it’s not as if they will be able to pass a far-ranging agenda with Trump still in office.) At the same time, however, we don’t necessarily know how these situations will pan out. Just because Hamilton says holding trials won’t be his focus, that doesn’t necessarily mean he would oppose his party’s move toward that or other accountability from Trump officials. Many of these Democrats are breaking with their party in potentially symbolic ways: They’re staking out a rhetorical difference without necessarily indicating that they would vote against the party on major issues that are likely to come up over the next two years. There is some evidence that Americans have warmed to the Democratic Party as these kinds of candidates have led the charge. A Gallup poll this week showed the party’s favorable rating rising to 43% — up from the mid-30s last year and 8 points higher than Republicans’ favorability. And the percentage of Americans who said the Democratic Party is “too liberal” has declined from 55% in 2022 to 46% today. But if Democrats do win either or both chambers in Congress, that new power could embolden the party’s left flank to try and assert themselves, leading to potential clashes within the party. To some degree, that’s the new reality for Democrats. There are simply more red states than blue states these days, and Trump won 24 of the 50 states by double digits. So if Democrats don’t run the table in swing states, they need to run moderate candidates who can win in pretty red territory. But that won’t make dealing with that tension any easier. Many in the party’s base have agonized over the sway that moderate former Democratic senators like Joe Manchin of West Virginia and Kyrsten Sinema of Arizona had as swing votes — and that Pennsylvania Sen. John Fetterman could have come next year. And there could be more where that came from.

title: Trump administration escalates voter roll fight with threats against California election officials
content: The Trump administration threatened to take legal action against California election officials if they did not review a list of alleged noncitizens on Los Angeles’ voter rolls within 48 hours, according to Tuesday letters from the Justice Department obtained by CNN. The letters , signed by the number two official at the Justice Department, are an escalation in DOJ’s attempts to press for aggressive voter purges with ballots already mailed out in some states, after courts have repeatedly pushed back at attempts by the administration to insert itself in the running of elections. It’s the latest step in a government-wide push to find voter fraud amid President Donald Trump’s baseless claims of widespread cheating in elections. The Justice Department is demanding that the election officials refuse to send ballots to the alleged noncitizen voters and is requesting that election officials segregate ballots from voters on the list until their citizenship is confirmed. Acting deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter wrote in the letters to the Los Angeles County registrar-recorder and the California Secretary of State that if election officials do not take steps to identify the alleged noncitizen voters, DOJ would “have no choice but to seek emergency relief.” McCotter wrote that the department provided a password-protected thumb drive containing names the administration “believes are likely non-citizens” who were sent a mail ballot this year. It requests that the election officials work with the Department of Homeland Security to comply with its demands. The letters were first reported by Reuters . Los Angeles County Registrar-Recorder Dean Logan said in a statement Wednesday that his office was reviewing the DOJ letter in coordination with California’s secretary of state and attorney general. Logan said that his office had not accessed the thumb drive provided by the federal government “because doing so would conflict with established data privacy and information security protocols.” The password for the thumb drive was handwritten on what appeared to be a blue post-it note attached to the bottom of the letter sent to Logan’s office on Tuesday. “We do not consider the device a secure medium,” he said. “Additionally, the letter does not specify the number of individuals involved or describe the information contained in the records.” A spokesperson for California Secretary of State Shirley Weber did not immediately respond to CNN’s inquiries. It is not clear what legal avenue the administration could use to force California election officials to take the actions it seeks. The Constitution gives states the primary job of running elections, though it allows Congress to pass some regulations of the vote as well. Earlier this summer, the Justice Department sent letters warning it would prosecute election officials who did not take adequate steps to remove noncitizens from voter registration files, but state officials of both parties dismissed the threat. It’s unclear why the Justice Department sent the letter now, as election officials view the window for changing protocols as closed. “California’s voter lists are public, and this administration has had 21 months with total control of the federal government to review those public lists,” said David Becker, a former DOJ voting section attorney who now advises election administrators. “California sent out mail ballots to all voters on Oct 5. One must question why the DOJ would violate its own rules about investigating elections close to Election Day, and over a week after they knew the state had already mailed ballots out, particularly when their past claims have been full of errors,” Becker said. The Justice Department defended sending the letters. “Federal law is clear: only American citizens may vote in federal elections. The Department will take all necessary legal action to protect election integrity and ensure compliance with federal law,” said DOJ spokesperson Kiersten Pels. The Trump administration has alleged there are hundreds of thousands of non-citizens on voter rolls. In August, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed DHS had identified 250,000 non-citizens registered to vote in four states — including California, along with Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Nevada — by comparing public voter rolls with federal immigration records. But those claims have come under immense scrutiny and, in some cases, failed to hold up . In Nevada, for instance, DHS acknowledged to state officials that its initial claim of 15,900 non-citizen registrants was an unvetted preliminary finding, and that it had only “confirmed” 185 of them through manual review. Last month, Nevada officials told DHS that their own subsequent review found all 185 were citizens — a conclusion DHS disputes. The Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division has also sought unredacted state voter roll data from the states as part of its hunt for noncitizens on the rolls. The department has sued 30 states demanding the data — but lost every case where a judge has ruled so far, including in California. Other attempts by the administration to police how states handle elections have also been shut down in court. The Supreme Court blocked a Trump directive for the US Postal Service to screen mail ballots, and a 2025 executive order from the president seeking to boost the proof of citizenship requirements for voter registration was halted in court as well. Trump’s efforts to implement those requirements through legislation faltered in Congress this year. A recent judge’s ruling dismissing a non-citizen voter prosecution the administration brought in Florida also has raised constitutional questions about the federal law barring non-citizen voting. The administration did secure a major legal win when the Supreme Court okayed a federal immigration data system that Trump has encouraged states to use to vet the citizenship status of their registered voters. Election officials in more than half of the states use the system voluntarily. However, even Republican election officials have balked at proposals from Justice Department that would force them to purge voters whom the administration has deemed ineligible — particularly given the accuracy concerns around the federal government’s data tools. This article has been updated with additional information.

title: Katie Zacharia presented herself as a lawyer. She’s not
content: The press secretary is supposed to spin the news, not be the news. On that most essential qualification, the new lead White House spokeswoman, Katie Zacharia, is struggling. She has presented herself as a lawyer but does not meet the requirements in her home state to use that title. And at least one watchdog group has asked the State Bar of California to investigate. It’s a development made even more awkward after Republicans mercilessly attacked the Democratic candidate for US Senate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed, for not being a doctor, though he went to medical school and made his career in public health. Zacharia has a law degree from the Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, but there’s no evidence she ever passed a bar exam. She does claim to have obtained a credential in China, but it’s not at all clear what credential she’s talking about. Squabbles over who can call themselves a lawyer or a doctor probably seem beside the point to a large portion of the country. This issue here is not that a law degree is required to be White House press secretary — it isn’t. The issue is that Zacharia has presented herself repeatedly on TV, including on CNN, as a lawyer, something the independent journalist Judd Legum first documented . Trump used the term “attorney” to describe her when he announced she would be his press secretary. A review by CNN’s K-File found at least six instances when she referred to herself as either a lawyer or a corporate lawyer in her own words and multiple other instances in which she posted or reposted to social media using the term attorney or “legal strategist.” Washington, DC, is filled to the brim with people who have law degrees but do not practice law. And it does not appear that Zacharia inappropriately tried to represent anyone in a court. But all of this does suggest the vetting operation at the White House is, to be charitable, not very thorough. When reporters asked Trump at the White House where Zacharia passed the bar, she chimed in from behind him that she was when she moved to China. Even Trump did a double take. Zacharia later told Politico she had “practiced international transactional law, with all the appropriate credentials.” It’s not clear — and the White House has not clarified — what certification Zacharia obtained in China, but it’s not the Chinese version of the bar exam. Only citizens can become licensed to practice law in China, according to the Ministry of Justice . Questions about Zacharia’s CV are also an awkward development since Republicans in Michigan have attacked the Democrat running for Senate there, Abdul El-Sayed, for not being a doctor despite having gone to medical school. At a debate this month, the Republican in the Senate race, former Rep. Mike Rogers, went so far as to say El-Sayed was a “con man.” As CNN has reported , El-Sayed earned a Doctor of Medicine from Columbia University, but he does not practice clinical medicine. El-Sayed has held public health positions in the Detroit area. His top policy issue is extending health insurance to all Americans. Democratic boosters of El-Sayed have continued to call him a doctor. “Abdul’s a doctor, and he’s taken on special interests to fight for good jobs, better healthcare, and lower costs,” former President Barack Obama said in an ad he cut for the Michigander. In addition to saying on TV that she is a lawyer, Zacharia cites some legal-sounding work on her LinkedIn page; for example, she lists herself as “general counsel” for the activist group Fix California. In the nonprofit group’s tax filing for 2024, Zacharia’s name appears as having been a fundraiser. She also lists herself as having worked as an “associate” in the international practice group at the Zhong Lun Law Firm in Beijing for nearly two years starting in 2011. The White House press corps, obviously, has followed up on this mystery. “Katie moved to China with her husband after graduating because of his job at an American private equity firm while she worked on international transaction law,” according to a White House official. CNN’s White House team has found no evidence that Zacharia has passed the bar exam in the states where she has lived and worked since graduating from Pepperdine. Here’s what California’s bar association told them: California law lays out what’s required to be a lawyer. There are requirements for college and law school, or their equivalents; for “good moral character”; passing an ethics exam; and passing the bar exam in California. Zacharia, as a result, should not be considered a lawyer in California, the state where she has lived and worked. A separate section of California law makes it a misdemeanor to pretend to be a lawyer. Here’s the language : Does presenting oneself as a lawyer on TV violate that piece of code? The group Campaign for Accountability, which describes itself as a nonpartisan government watchdog, on Wednesday announced it had asked the State Bar of California to investigate. Many other questions remain. What is the credential Zacharia obtained in China, if any? Did she try to take a bar exam and fail, or simply not take it? Why did no one at the White House, especially after questions arose about El-Sayed’s status as a doctor, think to follow up on this earlier? None of that really matters to anyone who is more concerned with how the White House is handling the war Trump launched on Iran or the related inflation that continues to hit Americans in the wallet. Questions about whether Zacharia can call herself a lawyer, or not, mostly distract from those other, larger issues. Ultimately, Trump is the person who speaks for his administration in the long, often rambling appearances he frequently makes in the Oval Office. But those appearances may become less enjoyable for him in the future, especially if Democrats take control of one or both chambers of Congress and, as expected, launch a series of investigations into his administration, the money his family has made during his presidency, and much more. He will, at that point, need a press secretary he can trust. CNN’s Andrew Kaczynski contributed reporting. This headline and story have been updated with additional reporting.

title: Republicans are playing defense — and it’s costing them
content: Republicans are spending hundreds of millions of dollars on advertising in battleground Senate races as they scramble to defend increasingly competitive GOP seats in the final stretch of the midterms. But when it comes to how far they can stretch a dollar, they’re effectively paying premium prices at Whole Foods while Democrats are shopping deals at Costco. Across nine of the most competitive Senate races last month, Republicans cumulatively outspent Democrats on broadcast TV ads by nearly 100% more, $233 million to $121 million, according to AdImpact data, but only saw about 40% more rating points. The disparity comes down to a difference in strategy. Republicans are relying heavily on outside groups, like super PACs, that pay elevated rates for ads and are making big buys late in the campaign, when inventory is stretched. By contrast, Democrats are taking advantage of discounted rates for candidates and earlier, less expensive reservations. At this stage in the game, Republicans are spending more to get less, which means the “shock and awe” of their massive dollar advantage isn’t necessarily translating to an actual impact on the ground, according to veteran Republican strategist John Thomas, who co-founded the government affairs firm Nestpoint. A better metric, he said, is to consider the gross rating points, or GRPs, a unit advertisers use to measure the reach and frequency of an ad campaign, independent of how much was paid for it. In those nine races – where outside groups accounted for about 9 in 10 Republican ad dollars, compared to about half for Democrats – Democrats paid $201 per GRP, while Republicans paid about $274. In some races in September, Democrats actually outpaced Republicans in GRPs, completely overcoming their spending edge. In North Carolina, for example, Republicans outspent Democrats by about $17 million to $14 million on TV ads in September, as former Gov. Roy Cooper poses a major threat to former RNC Chair Michael Whatley and the GOP chances of holding Sen. Thom Tillis’ seat. But Democrats got more than 71,000 GRPs from their spend while Republicans got about 58,000. And at the beginning of October – recognizing the costly, difficult road ahead for Whatley – Republicans actually began cutting their remaining ad bookings by about $15 million. Democrats were also outspent last month by Republicans in Maine by about 32%, another premier battleground race where former state Sen. Troy Jackson is looking to unseat veteran GOP incumbent Sen. Susan Collins, who has received major backing from national Republicans. But here, again, despite being outspent, Democrats got 6% more GRPs for their money. Even in Texas – where Democrats were blasted by Republican ad money in September, outspent more than 4 times over – the GRP gap was proportionally much smaller. Republicans got only 2.6 times more GRPs. A GOP super PAC had to spend more than $22 million to air its top ad , touting Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton ’s record as a prosecutor, about 15,500 times in September. Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico ’s campaign spent a little under $4 million to air its most aired ad , casting Paxton as “the most corrupt politician in Texas,” about 8,000 times. That amounts to less than one-fifth the spending for about half the airtime. Lauren French, communications director for Senate Majority PAC, a leading Democratic super PAC, also emphasized that buying TV late in the cycle becomes exorbitantly expensive. “The nitty-gritty of campaigning is that not all ad space costs the same,” she said. “If you are buying something in February, it’s going to be a lot cheaper, and you’re going to get a lot more bang for your buck than, say, if you’re buying it in September. So that’s why you’re seeing this huge disconnect between what Republicans are paying and what Democrats are paying on average in some of these races,” French said. In seven of the top nine Senate races by total TV and radio ad spending in September, Democrats paid less per GRP than Republicans. The two exceptions were New Hampshire and Alaska. Confident in their nominees, Republicans were able to secure comparable or better rates in both states’ key markets. In New Hampshire, this was reinforced by Republicans allocating relatively more to cheaper secondary markets. “Broadly speaking, Republicans are using their money pretty ineffectively, and public polling is saying that people are not seeing their ads as much as one would expect. So, by that definition alone, some of their money is being set on fire. We are being outspent in a lot of these states, which means we have to make more strategic decisions,” French said. Thomas said that Texas, in particular, was emblematic of this effect, with GOP outside groups mounting an urgent rescue effort for Paxton and pouring money into the state. He noted that Paxton allies had taken to buying ad time on national NFL broadcasts because local markets had grown so crowded. That’s why people across the country are seeing Texas Senate ads in games that don’t include the Dallas Cowboys or Houston Texans. “In some cases, because the commercial rate is so high in a local, like a Houston spot, it actually sometimes can be cheaper to buy a national spot,” he said. Democrats’ efficiency advantage might have been much greater, given their candidates have consistently raised more money their Republican opponents on a campaign-to-campaign basis, allowing them to spend more directly on their own ads at cheap rates. But thanks to a recent Supreme Court ruling , for the first time this year, national party committees can take advantage of candidate ad rates through coordinated buys. This means well-funded national committees like the National Republican Congressional Committee or National Republican Senate Committee can team up with candidates – like Mike Rogers in Michigan or Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio – and foot the bill for pricey ad campaigns while getting candidate discounts. The expansion of coordinated buying has allowed Republicans to blunt the Democratic candidate fundraising advantage. Democrats can do the same, but the GOP has taken to it far more aggressively: In September, GOP advertisers spent more than $30 million on coordinated ad buys, compared to about $5 million from Democrats. Outside groups like super PACs still play a dominant role, however, due to their unique ability to accept unlimited donations and make unlimited expenditures. “The money is actually very, very inefficient, but the benefit, even with the inefficiency of a super PAC, is one or two people can cut checks and fund the whole thing,” Thomas said. This story has been updated with additional information.

title: Nigel Farage says charities that help asylum seekers reach UK should be prosecuted
content: Charities and volunteers who help asylum seekers get to the UK should face potential criminal prosecution, Nigel Farage has said in an interview with a rightwing US podcaster. While the Reform UK leader did not specify which organisations should be targeted, he and other senior Reform figures have been heavily critical of the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), which has faced a campaign of intimidation for its work in rescuing asylum seekers in the Channel. Speaking to Benny Johnson , a podcaster who has previously written for a series of rightwing US outlets, including Breitbart News, Farage discussed the arrival of asylum seekers on small boats, calling it “literally an invasion of people who could cause us enormous harm”. Johnson asked him: “Do you believe in criminal penalties for those who facilitated this invasion of the English Isles?” Farage replied: “Totally, totally. The role of the NGOs, the role of those that are sponsored by taxpayers’ money, because they’re nice, they’re good, they’re kind. They have actually aided and abetted criminality in absolutely every way. “These are people [who are] are deluded – deluded, hard-left socialist Marxists, who don’t believe in countries, don’t believe in borders, don’t believe in identities, are intent on destroying everything that exists.” Farage has previously described the RNLI, which rescues some asylum seekers, a small proportion of its lifesaving work, as a “migrant taxi service”, while other Reform figures have criticised the charity, including sharing footage of far-right protesters abusing RNLI crews bringing people ashore. Calling for charities and campaign groups to be prosecuted for their work has echoes of the efforts by the former Hungarian prime minister Viktor Orbán to try to cement his grip on power. A Reform spokesperson said Farage’s comments “speak for themselves”. In his conversation with Johnson, Farage repeatedly raised what he said was the issue of Muslim asylum seekers arriving in the UK, citing what the example of Michigan, the US state where rightwing agitators have sought to whip up anti-Muslim feeling. Farage said: “We are importing into our countries … people who will do us enormous harm, who will change, disrupt our lives in every way, in fact make our way of life potentially unrecognisable.” Saying that European countries such as the UK and France had a greater problem with migration than the US, Farage said if Donald Trump was followed in office by a “weak politician” who did not tackle migration and stand up for “American, English-speaking Christian values” then the consequences would be dire. Farage told Johnson: “If we don’t, this show of yours will be illegal in five or 10 years’ time. Literally, you’ll be banned for hate speech.” Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Elsewhere in the interview, Farage speculated that five UK nationals arrested near RAF Fairford late last month before being bailed had been undertaking “a dummy run for a proper terrorist attack on UK forces”. He added: “I’m deeply, deeply shocked that they’re out on bail whilst there are other people in this country who have said things that the establishment now thinks are racist, who are held inside behind bars without, frankly, proper charge. So it’s what we call here two-tier policing.” Farage has a habit of sometimes making his message more robust for rightwing US audiences. He has appeared several times on the web TV show hosted by the disgraced far-right pundit Alex Jones, who was sued by bereaved parents of the 2012 Sandy Hook school shooting , which Jones said had been a hoax. Farage was criticised by some Jewish groups for using these and other US interviews to discuss tropes and conspiracy theories associated with the far right and antisemitism.

title: UK’s ‘incoherent’ approach to China plagued by lack of expertise, report says
content: The UK’s approach to China is “beset by incoherence” and plagued by a lack of senior expertise, according to a report warning of the risks inherent in misjudging the bilateral relationship. An audit by the Inter-Parliamentary Alliance on China (Ipac), an international grouping of China-sceptic legislators, says past engagement with Beijing has often exposed the UK to the risks of interference without delivering the opportunities promised. “Successful UK engagement with China must always be framed by an understanding that the PRC (People’s Republic of China) is an inherently hostile authoritarian state that does not share our values,” an underlined sentence in the audit, published on Wednesday, reads. The inherent power imbalance in the relationship with the world’s second largest economy is “further compounded by muddled policy and weak engagement”, it says. It cites the example of a visiting Chinese delegation who had noted that no one who engaged with Beijing at a senior level in government was a Mandarin speaker, or had significant experience of living in China. Although British expertise exists, it is often siloed and “not translated into capability”, says Ipac, pointing to budget cuts as an additional problem. Ipac counts almost 50 MPs among its members, including from Labour, the Conservatives, the Liberal Democrats, the Scottish National party, the Greens and Reform. Ipac member and former security minister Tom Tugendhat said the report was “a clear-eyed and realistic take on the defining foreign policy problem of this century, filling a gap left by years of policy neglect”. A UK government spokesperson said that while working with China presented opportunities, “we are also clear-eyed about the threats China poses, and national security is the first duty of government”. “We will cooperate with China where we can while meeting any challenges head-on,” they added. The Chinese embassy in London said Ipac’s “sole agenda is to manufacture falsehoods, mislead the public, and undermine China’s relations with other countries”. The report “distorts the facts” and “is not even worth refuting”, it added. While the Ipac report accepts that “disengagement is not an option”, it advocates for clearly defined red lines around issues such as critical infrastructure, frontier technologies and human rights. The document offers several recommendations, including better institutional coordination, the strengthened use of national security tools, and diversification of supply chains. Emerging technologies such as AI represent “another front we’re potentially facing”, Labour’s Dame Meg Hillier said at the launch, with the report identifying areas of concern such as disinformation and surveillance capabilities. Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion The climate crisis is identified as a low-risk area for cooperation and alignment. “Climate targets as set will not be met without cooperation with China, and accepting medium-term dependence. This means accepting supply chains tainted by forced labour and unfair trade practices,” the audit says. The government conducted its own audit of the UK-China relationship in late 2024 but has said it cannot publish most of the detail for fear of damaging national interests. But Evan Fowler, author of the Ipac report, said that a public audit was important “because engagement with China doesn’t just happen at the government level”. It was “very welcome” that there was an understanding that better language skills were needed to deal with China, said Kerry Brown, a former diplomat and director of the Lau China Institute at King’s College London. However, he said, “the critical issue now is lived experience” in China. “Some of the members of Ipac … are really keen on promoting this very security-oriented idea that going to China is in some ways opening you up to exposure,” he said. “You can’t teach really important things in a classroom; you can only go and learn them through daily life … and that is the thing that is very difficult to do now, and it’s also the thing that doesn’t seem to be supported.”

title: New UK sanctions powers will enable action against supporters of illegal Israeli settlements
content: The UK is expanding its sanctions powers to freeze assets and target entities enabling illegal Israeli settlements, obstructing humanitarian aid or unlawfully holding prisoners. The statutory instrument introducing the global human rights and international humanitarian law sanctions adds three new grounds to the 2020 regime: serious violations of international humanitarian law, obstruction of humanitarian assistance and serious violations of the right to liberty and security of person. Unlawful settlement activity will be captured through a breach of international humanitarian law, including the Geneva convention on occupation. The Israeli government closed the UK consulate last week in protest, forcing the it to withdraw 21 diplomats and downgrade the consulate to the status of a mission. But the Israeli punishment does not appear to have deterred the UK government. The proposed new powers also extend government reach beyond direct perpetrators of wrongdoing to those who facilitate, incite, promote or support qualifying conduct, provide it with finance, goods or technology, conceal evidence of it or benefit from it. Banks and commercial entities could also fall within this remit as designation only requires reasonable grounds to suspect involvement. The proposed sanctions measures include asset freezes and prohibitions on making funds or economic resources available, travel bans and director disqualifications. A new urgent procedure will allow ministers to mirror designations already made by the EU, US, Canada or Australia for up to 112 days while a specific separate UK case is prepared. The new global sanctions regime will come into force on Thursday but will need endorsement by MPs and peers within 28 days. The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband , is pushing through the measures at speed because the Israeli government has vowed to press ahead with an E1 settlement containing 1,234 homes in the West Bank – a development that many observers say would sever a contiguous, viable Palestinian state, so making the so-called two-state solution to the Palestinian-Israeli conflict near impossible. The E1 bids close on 19 October but the Israel Land Authority has confirmed that the tender box will not be opened, nor the bids considered, before 19 November, which is after the Israeli election on 27 October. The British Palestinian Project said the Israeli deferral “does not remove the need to deter commitments being made now, since bidders and their backers commit on 19 October, contracts could still be signed before a new Israeli government is formed”. Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion The project welcomed the addition of the right to liberty and security of person in the new laws, saying it opens a route to sanctions for serious arbitrary or unlawful detention, including of Palestinian children, and of those responsible for or enabling it. Save the Children estimated in November 2023 that 10,000 Palestinian children had passed through Israeli military detention over the preceding 20 years. A UN 2026 report on children and armed conflict verified that 981 Palestinian children were detained by Israeli forces in 2025 and 180 of them remained in administrative detention without charge or trial at the year’s end. The UK has already applied sanctions designations for restrictions on humanitarian aid in Sudan and South Sudan but this is the first time this general power is being applied as part of a new worldwide regime including Israel. Refusing permits or blocking convoys will be sufficient grounds to apply sanctions, without requiring the obstruction to constitute a formal breach of international humanitarian law – thereby lowering the threshold for action. Separate work is under way by UK officials in conjunction with European partners on how to outlaw British trade with unlawful Israeli settlements.

title: That Kemi is spectacularly wrong about almost everything is a big help to the PM
content: L ittle things please little minds. And minds don’t come much smaller than some of those in Westminster. If a researcher had come up with a study that showed one element two points higher in value than countless other experiments, it would almost certainly be marked down either as an outlier or “within the margin of error”. At the very least, no conclusions would be drawn until many other experiments had been conducted which had produced similar results. Serious scientific journals would just laugh at you if you asked them to publish your findings. And yet. In one – just one out of many – recent opinion poll, the Tories have increased their ratings by a couple of points and are now for the first time in years in second place, ahead of Reform. And all of a sudden, Kemi Badenoch is insisting this is incontrovertible proof that the Tories are back in business. All the sins of its 14 years in government have been wiped clean. All hail to Kemi, the new chief. She is the chosen one. And the Conservatives are a government-in-waiting. You need a certain amount of self-confidence to make it as a party leader. Not to say a touch of the Panglossian. The ability to insist all is well when it is turning to shit. But you can have too much of a good thing. You must at least be within touching distance of reality. And it appears that once again Kemi has jumped the shark. The one good poll has gone to her head and she now believes she is invincible. Nothing can touch her narcissism. In her early days as Tory leader, Kemi used to crash and burn every week at prime minister’s questions. She considered preparation and research to be beneath her. Instead, she peddled the latest conspiracy theories she had seen on X with a series of scattergun questions. She only started to improve when her minders tried to get her to concentrate for 10 minutes of sustained questions on one subject. Yet over the conference break, Kemi has undergone a brain wipe. She is back in her happy space of making it up as she goes along. No one knows better than Kemi. Sadly for the Tory leader, Kemi’s approach is also Andy Burnham’s happy place. Much more of this and the prime minister is going to look forward to his Wednesday lunchtime encounters in the Commons. Never look an easy win in the eye. Not because he’s word perfect – there are still a lot of unanswered questions about his involvement with the Manchester City owners – but because there’s an engaging openness to him you seldom find in other politicians. A willingness to answer the questions and to appear as if he’s listening. Mr Congeniality. It’s also a big help to Andy that Kemi is spectacularly wrong about almost everything. Arguments are always so much simpler when your opponents are deluded. Indeed you couldn’t escape the irony of her insisting that it was Burnham who was consistently mistaken about everything. Even the head of MI5, Ken McCallum, had slapped the prime minister down for suggesting hostile actors had interfered with the Brexit referendum. Kemi can’t bear the fact she might have had the backing of the Russian state in 2016. Burnham chose to respond to Kemi in the most hurtful way. With kindness. No anger. Just a gentle reiteration of the facts. It was incontrovertible that Russia had tried to influence both the 2019 general election and the EU referendum. The evidence was in front of our eyes. Russian bots selling misinformation all over social media. It was a non-story. And far from correcting him, McCallum had gone out of his way to confirm this. And who had been keeping the story alive for a third day by bringing it up at PMQs? Take a bow, Kemi. The Tory leader seemingly content to carry on doing the Russians’ dirty work for them. At least Nathan Gill, Reform’s former leader in Wales, had the sense to get paid for this. Kemi was doing it for free. Andy ended by saying he would be delighted to debate whether Brexit had done more harm than good. Kemi shook her head. This isn’t an argument the Tories are keen to have. Their feeling is Brexit is something we all just have to suck up. After that, Kemi looked a bit lost. Clueless. Scouring her file for something to ask. Instead she just wasted her own and everyone else’s time. First by asking about the budget. As if Burnham was ever going to say: “You know what? Since you’ve asked I might as well give you a heads-up two weeks early.” All Kemi achieved was to make herself look half witted. She ended up sounding a bit hurt. She had hoped that Andy would have spent more time problem-solving than point-scoring. There are days with Kemi when even giving a straight answer comes across as point-scoring. Earlier in the day, Dominic Cummings had been giving evidence to a Lords select committee on how to prevent rogue actors from entering No 10. That should have been a very short session. Just stop morons like Boris Johnson from appointing people like Dom as his special adviser. Curiously this hadn’t occurred to Dom, nor to the dopey peers interrogating him. It was a bizarre hour and a half. The sort that gives you mild PTSD. Your mind goes back to all the damage he did to the country during the Brexit referendum and during his year in No 10 and suddenly the horror floods back. Just when your brain has done its best to forget all about him. To consider him a footnote in history. For the record, Dom is as deluded as ever. His main thesis seemed to be that Boris was right to allow him to do whatever he liked but no one else in No 10 should ever be allowed to do what he did. Some things never change. We are well rid of him.

title: Reform UK councillors and candidates filmed making racist and extreme comments
content: Reform UK has been rocked by a fresh crisis after councillors and election candidates for the party were caught on film making graphic threats of extreme violence and expressing racist and misogynistic views. Three councillors have already stood down from the party, which said it was conducting an investigation over the first revelations from an ITV undercover investigation that aired on Wednesday. Reform leader Nigel Farage has postponed a major announcement that was due to take place in Essex on Thursday morning as the party tries to contain the fallout expected to come from further revelations in the coming days. That will include revelations from undercover filming of senior Reform politicians and officials working at its UK headquarters. Farage has made repeated pledges over the last two years to rid Reform of “extremists” and “bigots” and introduce vetting. The party says it carries out vetting checks on everyone who wants to stand for election. However, the first clips from ITV’s year-long undercover investigation showed Alan Feeney, a Reform councillor and deputy mayor of Solihull, calling Asian homeowners “parasites,” and stating that “no more than 1% of [the] British population can be non-white”. Feeney won seats on Birmingham city council and Solihull Metropolitan borough council and was then appointed deputy mayor of Solihull. He has announced that he has left Reform “for personal reasons”. Other candidates were recorded making comments of extreme violence and sharing deeply misogynistic and racist views, including a Bromley councillor calling for King Charles to be killed and another councillor who made disturbing sexual and misogynistic comments about female colleagues. Feeney was filmed with other candidates who went on to become councillors, Jamie Campbell and Chris Whelan, talking about where a local mosque might be built. After they make extreme racist comments in the discussion, Feeney says: “Oh god, we’re all going to end up in the papers”. Chris Whelan announced he had resigned from Reform on 12 October “on personal and health grounds”. Campbell is still in post. Dean Miller, a Reform councillor for Bromley, was filmed separately making a range of comments during campaigning for the Makerfield byelection, including when he discussed what he would do with illegal immigrants crossing the Channel. Reform has been attempting to pre-empt the impact from the ITV investigation, which will potentially be at its most damaging when footage from inside Reform’s London HQ airs. The party used a statement issued on Wednesday night to accuse ITV and Hardcash Productions of “extreme methods of deception”. “They have infiltrated our workplace including commissioning an undercover journalist to provide altered identification documents, a false address, and false credentials so that they could be given access to Reform’s headquarters, computer systems, and spy on its employees,” it said. The party said that this came at a time when Farage and other members of Reform were “being targeted by individuals who wished them harm and caused a security issue which was documented during the course of the undercover investigation”. “They have not included this in their report, despite being on notice since March this year. There is currently an ongoing police investigation relating to security breaches against Mr Farage, as is well known,” it added. Reform said that not all individuals covertly recorded by ITV are members of Reform UK, adding: “Where members, activists and councillors have clearly behaved inappropriately, investigations have commenced. In some cases, there have been suspensions and due process must be followed.” The latest crisis to hit the party comes at a time when it has been stalling in the polls and faces problems including the fallout from a different undercover investigation which filmed senior officials discussing a potential way to secure foreign donations to the party . The outcome is also awaited of a parliamentary standards commissioner investigation into whether Farage should have declared a £5m gift from the crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne . Bridget Phillipson MP, chair of the Labour party, said: “The extreme racism and appalling behaviour exposed by this investigation is truly sickening. Nigel Farage can’t shrug these latest revelations off as being a few bad apples. Every Reform councillor, council candidate or party member found to have made such despicable comments must be thrown out of Reform UK immediately.” Undercover: A Year in Reform, airs on 18 October at 10.20pm on ITV1, ITVX, STV & STV Player
